name: Crème de Cacao
description: Cacao bean and vanilla liqueur, made clear (white) or caramel-coloured (dark) from the same base. The crème refers to sugar content, not dairy — there is no cream in it at all.
funFact: EU rules require a crème liqueur to carry at least 250 grams of sugar per litre, which is where the name comes from — the texture, not the ingredient.

serve.how: Rarely drunk neat. White goes into a Grasshopper and an Alexander; dark into a Brandy Alexander or a Twentieth Century. Keep the white version when you need chocolate flavour without muddying the colour of a drink.

composition.summary: Cacao beans and vanilla infused into neutral spirit and heavily sweetened.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Infused or distilled, then sweetened; dark is caramel-coloured

composition.process: Distilling rather than infusing gives the white version, since the colour stays behind in the beans.

name: Crème de Banane
description: Banana liqueur, bright yellow and frankly artificial-tasting in its cheap forms, genuinely good in its better ones. A tiki staple and the making of a Banana Daiquiri.
funFact: Isoamyl acetate, the compound that reads as banana, is also produced naturally by fermenting yeast — which is why some Jamaican rums taste of banana with no banana involved.

serve.how: In a Banana Daiquiri with rum and lime, or a bar spoon in a tiki build where it bridges rum and citrus. Neat it is very sweet; the better bottlings made from real fruit are worth seeking out.

composition.summary: Banana infused into neutral spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Banana, natural or compounded, plus vanilla

composition.process: Real-fruit versions are darker and less neon than the compounded ones, and taste noticeably less like confectionery.

name: Crème de Mûre
description: Blackberry liqueur, deep purple and tart under the sweetness. Without it there is no Bramble, which is the only cocktail invented in 1980s London that anyone still orders.
funFact: Dick Bradsell built the Bramble at Fred's Club in Soho, drizzling the mûre over crushed ice so it bleeds down through the drink.

serve.how: Drizzled over a gin sour on crushed ice to make a Bramble — pour it last and do not stir, the bleed is the point. It also lifts a Kir if you want something darker than cassis.

composition.summary: Blackberries macerated in neutral spirit and sweetened.
composition.process: Like cassis, it is a maceration rather than a distillate, so the fruit character stays raw and bright.

name: Crème de Noyaux
description: Made from apricot and cherry stones rather than nuts, which gives an almond flavour from a fruit source. Pink, old-fashioned, and the ingredient that makes a Pink Squirrel pink.
funFact: The almond note comes from benzaldehyde in the kernels — the same compound that makes marzipan taste of almond, present here without a single almond involved.

serve.how: A cocktail ingredient rather than a sipper. It is the almond note in a Pink Squirrel and an Old Etonian, and it substitutes for orgeat in drinks where you want alcohol rather than syrup.

composition.summary: Apricot and cherry kernels macerated in spirit and sweetened.
composition.process: Kernels contain amygdalin, which is why the quantity used is carefully controlled.

name: Melon Liqueur
description: Bright green muskmelon liqueur, invented in Japan in 1978 and responsible for an entire decade of drinks. Sweet, unmistakable, and rehabilitated in recent years by bartenders who stopped being embarrassed by it.
funFact: Suntory launched it in 1978 and the colour comes entirely from added dye — the melon infusion itself is pale gold.

serve.how: With soda and lime over ice, which is far better than its reputation. In cocktails it makes a Midori Sour or a Japanese Slipper. Cut it with acid; the sugar needs something to push against.

composition.summary: Muskmelon infused into neutral spirit, sweetened and coloured.
composition.process: Two melon varieties are used, one for aroma and one for body.

name: Black Raspberry Liqueur
description: Black raspberries, blackberries, vanilla and honey infused into cognac, from the Loire. Sold in a round bottle bound like a medieval orb, and rather better than the packaging suggests.
funFact: The recipe is said to descend from a raspberry liqueur served to Louis XIV when he visited the Loire in the seventeenth century.

serve.how: Topped with champagne as a Kir Royale variant, or in a French Martini with vodka and pineapple. Neat over ice it is heavy going — it wants dilution and acid.

composition.summary: Berries infused into cognac with vanilla and honey.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Black raspberry, blackberry, Madagascar vanilla, honey

composition.process: A cognac base rather than neutral spirit is what gives it weight behind the fruit.

name: Coconut Rum Liqueur
description: Caribbean rum flavoured with coconut and cut to around 21%. Dismissed for decades as a holiday drink, and quietly indispensable in any tiki bar that wants coconut without opening a fresh nut.
funFact: It was created in 1978 specifically to make Piña Coladas easier to serve at bar speed, which is exactly what it still does.

serve.how: With pineapple juice, or long with soda and lime. In a Piña Colada it replaces both the rum and the cream of coconut in a hurry. Keep it cold; warm it turns cloying fast.

composition.summary: Caribbean rum blended with coconut extract and sweetened.
composition.process: The rum base is real and aged, which is why it mixes better than a neutral coconut liqueur would.

name: Anisette
description: The sweetest of the anise family, made from green anise seed and heavily sugared. Softer than pastis and lower in strength than ouzo, and a Mediterranean breakfast habit for older generations.
funFact: Marie Brizard began making it in Bordeaux in 1755 from a recipe she was reportedly given by a West Indian sailor she had nursed through illness.

serve.how: With cold water, which turns it milky, or over ice. In Italy and Spain it also goes into coffee. It is sweeter than pastis, so use less of it and more water than instinct suggests.

composition.summary: Green anise seed distilled into neutral spirit and heavily sweetened.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Green anise seed, sometimes coriander and fennel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled with the seed, then sugared

composition.process: The higher sugar is what separates it from pastis and ouzo more than the botanicals do.

name: Chinchón
description: Spain's protected anise spirit, from the town of Chinchón south of Madrid, made in dry, sweet and extra-strength versions. Distilled from anise grown locally rather than flavoured after the fact.
funFact: The seco especial is bottled at 74%, which makes it one of the strongest commercially available anise spirits anywhere.

serve.how: Dry over ice as an aperitif, sweet after a meal, and the 74% version with considerable respect and a great deal of water. Spaniards also add it to coffee as a carajillo.

composition.summary: Locally grown anise distilled in copper alembics.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper alembic, distilled with the seed

composition.process: Distilling with the seed rather than adding oil afterwards is what earns it protected status.

name: Herbsaint
description: New Orleans' anise spirit, created in 1934 as a legal substitute for absinthe when the real thing was still banned. It is what a Sazerac is rinsed with in its home city.
funFact: The name is a contraction of herbe sainte, the Creole French name for wormwood — a fairly transparent nod to what it was standing in for.

serve.glass: Used as a rinse; or a tumbler with water
serve.how: Rinse a chilled glass and discard the excess, then build a Sazerac in it. Neat it takes water like pastis and louches the same way. The Original formula is drier and closer to the pre-war recipe.

composition.summary: Anise and fennel distilled into neutral spirit, wormwood-free at first.
composition.process: It was built to satisfy absinthe drinkers under a legal regime that banned the original, and it never lost that job.

name: Kümmel
description: Caraway, cumin and fennel in a clear, sweet liqueur with roots in sixteenth-century Holland and a devoted afterlife in Scottish golf clubhouses, where it is drunk against the shakes.
funFact: It is known in British golfing circles as the putting mixture, on the widely held theory that it steadies the hands.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer in a small glass, or over ice. It also works in a Silver Bullet with gin and lemon. The caraway is assertive, so it divides a room much as aquavit does.

composition.summary: Caraway and cumin distilled into neutral spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled with the seed, then sweetened

composition.process: It shares its botanical backbone with aquavit; the difference is the sugar.

name: Cinnamon Schnapps
description: Neutral spirit heavily flavoured with cinnamon, sometimes carrying flakes of gold leaf. Bracing, sweet and hot, and the single most-ordered shot in a great many bars.
funFact: The gold-flake versions descend from Danziger Goldwasser, a sixteenth-century tradition of suspending edible gold in liqueur as a supposed medicine.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer, in one. Cold is essential — warm, the sugar dominates and the cinnamon turns medicinal. It also does real work in hot cider or a mulled drink.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit flavoured with cinnamon and sweetened.
composition.process: Cassia rather than true Ceylon cinnamon gives the sharper, hotter note the category is built on.

name: Parfait Amour
description: A violet-purple liqueur of citrus, rose petals, vanilla and almond, made since the eighteenth century and once sold as a love potion. More perfume than drink, and used accordingly.
funFact: It was marketed in the 1700s as an aphrodisiac, which is where the name — perfect love — comes from.

serve.how: A cocktail ingredient rather than a sipper. A bar spoon adds colour and floral lift to a gin sour; more than that and the drink tastes of soap. Sits close to crème de violette but with citrus behind it.

composition.summary: Citrus peel, rose and violet infused into spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Curaçao orange peel, rose petals, violet, vanilla, almond

composition.process: It is essentially a curaçao with flowers, which is why the citrus is still detectable under the perfume.

name: Pistachio Liqueur
description: Sicilian pistachios, mostly from Bronte on the slopes of Etna, blended into a cream or clear liqueur. Intensely nutty, and a relatively modern addition to the Italian liqueur canon.
funFact: Bronte pistachios grow in volcanic soil on Etna, are harvested only every other year, and cost several times the price of ordinary pistachios.

serve.how: Straight from the fridge in a small glass after dinner, or poured over gelato. The cream versions separate if frozen, so chill rather than freeze.

composition.summary: Roasted pistachios infused into spirit, often with cream.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Bronte pistachios, sugar, sometimes cream and vanilla

composition.process: Roasting the nuts before maceration is what pushes it from green and raw to rounded.

name: Nocello
description: A walnut and hazelnut liqueur from Emilia-Romagna, lighter and less syrupy than nocino, which is made from green walnuts. This one uses ripe nuts, so it reads as toasted rather than bitter.
funFact: Its cousin nocino is made from green walnuts picked at midsummer, husks and all, which is why nocino is bitter and this is not.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, over ice, or poured onto vanilla gelato. It also works in coffee and stands in well for Frangelico when you want walnut rather than pure hazelnut.

composition.summary: Ripe walnuts and hazelnuts infused into neutral spirit.
composition.process: Ripe nuts rather than green ones is the entire distinction from nocino.

name: Blood Orange Liqueur
description: Made from Sicilian blood oranges grown on Etna's slopes, with the fruit's characteristic raspberry note intact. Deeper and less bitter than a curaçao, and a genuinely different thing from triple sec.
funFact: Blood oranges get their colour from anthocyanins that only develop when nights are cold, which is why Etna's altitude matters to the crop.

serve.how: Over ice with soda, or in place of triple sec in a Margarita or Sidecar where it brings berry as well as citrus. At 40% it has enough backbone to be sipped neat over a cube.

composition.summary: Blood orange peel and juice distilled and blended into neutral spirit.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Sanguinello and Tarocco blood oranges, plus lemon

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Peel distilled, juice blended in afterwards

composition.process: Higher strength than most orange liqueurs, which is why it holds up in a stirred drink.

name: Bergamot Liqueur
description: Made from the Calabrian bergamot, a citrus grown almost nowhere else and best known for flavouring Earl Grey tea. Floral, bitter and unmistakably perfumed.
funFact: Around 80% of the world's bergamot comes from a narrow coastal strip of Calabria, and the fruit is grown almost entirely for its oil rather than to eat.

serve.how: Cold and neat after dinner, or a bar spoon in a gin sour where it does what a tea infusion would without the tannin. It is bitter enough to work as an aperitif over ice with soda.

composition.summary: Bergamot peel infused into neutral spirit and sweetened.
composition.process: The fruit is too sour and bitter to eat, so essentially the entire crop goes to oil and liqueur.

name: Ratafia Catalana
description: A Catalan liqueur of green walnuts and dozens of herbs, macerated in the sun through summer and traditionally started on the feast of Saint John. Made at home across Catalonia to family recipes.
funFact: The jars are traditionally left outdoors for the whole of summer, so the maceration is driven by sunlight rather than heat from a still.

serve.how: Neat after a meal, at cellar temperature. Catalans serve it with dessert and at village festivals. Sweet and heavily spiced, so a small pour goes far.

composition.summary: Green walnuts and herbs sun-macerated in spirit with sugar.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Green walnuts, cinnamon, nutmeg, lemon peel, dozens of herbs

composition.process: Nou de Sant Joan — walnuts picked around 24 June, while the shell is still soft enough to cut.

name: Palo de Mallorca
description: A Mallorcan bitter of gentian root and cinchona bark, dark as treacle and originally sold as an anti-malarial when the island's wetlands still carried the disease.
funFact: It was drunk to ward off malaria in the Mallorcan marshlands, and survived the disease's eradication purely because islanders had grown to like it.

serve.how: Over ice with soda and a slice of lemon, which is the standard island serve. Neat it is thick and very sweet. Locals also drink it with orange juice.

composition.summary: Gentian and cinchona infused in spirit with caramelised sugar.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Gentian root, cinchona bark, burnt sugar

composition.process: The burnt sugar gives both the colour and most of the body.

name: Guavaberry Liqueur
description: Sint Maarten's national liqueur, made from wild guavaberries that ripen only briefly in the island's hills — a fruit unrelated to guava despite the name. Rum-based, spiced, and a Christmas tradition.
funFact: There is a traditional Christmas carol on the island whose entire subject is going house to house asking for a taste of the family's guavaberry.

serve.how: Neat in a small glass, or over ice. Islanders drink it at Christmas and mix it with rum punch. The wild fruit is picked from hillside trees rather than farmed, so supply is genuinely limited.

composition.summary: Wild guavaberries steeped in aged rum with spice and sugar.
composition.process: The berry has nothing to do with guava; it is a myrtle relative that fruits for a few weeks a year.

name: Sorrel Liqueur
description: Made from hibiscus calyces — sorrel in Caribbean usage — steeped with rum, ginger and clove. Deep crimson, tart and spiced, and inseparable from Christmas across the West Indies.
funFact: The plant is Hibiscus sabdariffa, the same species that makes agua de Jamaica in Mexico and karkade in Egypt — three continents, one calyx.

serve.how: Cold over ice, or topped with sparkling wine. It is tart enough not to need much cutting. Caribbean households make it fresh each December and the bought version is a year-round stand-in.

composition.summary: Hibiscus calyces steeped with rum, ginger and spice.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Dried hibiscus calyces, ginger, clove, cinnamon, orange peel

composition.process: It is the calyx that is used, not the flower — the fleshy cup left after the bloom drops.

name: Ponche Kuba
description: A Caribbean cream liqueur of rum, condensed milk, egg and spice, from Curaçao and hugely popular across Venezuela and the Dutch islands. Thicker and more cinnamon-driven than Irish cream.
funFact: It is a Christmas fixture across the southern Caribbean, where it competes directly with Venezuela's ponche crema for the same place on the table.

serve.how: Cold from the fridge, neat, in a small glass. Shake before pouring. It also goes into coffee, and over ice cream. Refrigerate once opened and finish it reasonably quickly.

composition.summary: Rum blended with condensed milk, egg and spice.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Condensed milk, egg, cinnamon, nutmeg, vanilla

composition.process: Condensed milk rather than fresh cream is what makes it shelf-stable in the tropics.

name: Licor de Café
description: Costa Rican coffee liqueur, built on cane spirit and Tarrazú beans, drier and more roast-forward than the Mexican coffee liqueurs that dominate the shelf.
funFact: Tarrazú beans grow between 1,200 and 1,900 metres, and the altitude is what gives the acidity that survives into the liqueur.

serve.how: Over ice, or with milk. It is less sweet than Kahlúa, which makes it the better choice in an Espresso Martini where you want coffee rather than sugar. Costa Ricans also add it to hot coffee.

composition.summary: Costa Rican coffee extracted into cane spirit and sweetened.
composition.process: Less sugar than the Mexican style is the whole difference, and it shows in cocktails.

name: Yuzushu
description: Japanese yuzu steeped in shochu or sake, cloudy with pulp and intensely aromatic. Yuzu is barely edible as a fruit — almost all peel and pip — which is exactly why it works as a liqueur.
funFact: Yuzu trees can take a decade to fruit, and the fruit is so pithy that a kilo yields very little juice — which is why it is priced like a spice.

serve.how: Over ice, or with soda in a highball. Shake the bottle first; the pulp settles and it is most of the flavour. Low in alcohol, so it drinks like a long aperitif rather than a digestive.

composition.summary: Yuzu fruit and peel steeped in shochu or sake and sweetened.
composition.process: The peel carries the aroma, so the fruit goes in whole rather than juiced.

name: Maesil-ju
description: Korean green plum liqueur, made by steeping unripe maesil plums in soju with sugar. Sweeter and rounder than Japanese umeshu, made from the same fruit and a different tradition.
funFact: Maesil and ume are the same fruit, Prunus mume, which is neither plum nor apricot but sits somewhere between the two.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or over ice, after a meal. Koreans also drink it with soda. It is sweeter than umeshu, so it works better as a dessert pour than an aperitif.

composition.summary: Unripe maesil plums steeped in soju with sugar.
composition.process: The fruit must be unripe; ripe maesil ferments rather than infusing cleanly.

name: Lychee Liqueur
description: Lychee infused into neutral spirit, floral and perfumed to the point of tasting artificial even when it is not. Responsible for the entire 2000s vogue for the Lychee Martini.
funFact: Lychee's characteristic aroma comes partly from rose oxide, the same compound that makes roses and some Gewürztraminer wines smell as they do.

serve.how: In a Lychee Martini with vodka, or topped with sparkling wine. It needs acid — a squeeze of lime keeps it from reading as syrup. Neat it is very sweet.

composition.summary: Lychee fruit infused into neutral spirit and sweetened.
composition.process: The floral note is fragile and the better producers avoid heat entirely in production.

name: Ginger Liqueur
description: Fresh ginger macerated into a spirit base, often with cognac or eau-de-vie behind it. Hot, sweet and considerably more useful behind a bar than its shelf presence suggests.
funFact: Gingerol, the compound responsible for the burn, converts to the milder zingerone when heated — which is why cooked ginger is sweeter than raw.

serve.how: Over ice with soda and lime, or as a modifier in a whisky sour where it does the work of both sweetener and spice. It also improves a Moscow Mule considerably.

composition.summary: Fresh ginger macerated into a brandy or neutral spirit base.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Fresh ginger root, citrus, sometimes vanilla

composition.process: Cold maceration preserves the raw burn that heat would soften.

name: Apricot Brandy Liqueur
description: Not a brandy at all in most bottles but an apricot liqueur, which causes endless confusion with classic cocktail recipes. Sweet, stone-fruited, and essential to a great many pre-war drinks.
funFact: Old cocktail books calling for apricot brandy almost always mean the liqueur, not a true fruit distillate — substituting a dry eau-de-vie wrecks the drink.

serve.how: A cocktail ingredient. It is in a Pendennis Club, a Charlie Chaplin and countless tiki builds. If a vintage recipe calls for apricot brandy, reach for this rather than a Marillenbrand.

composition.summary: Apricots and kernels infused into brandy or neutral spirit.
composition.process: Kernels supply the almond note; flesh alone tastes flat and jammy.

name: Sea Buckthorn Liqueur
description: Made from a fiercely tart orange berry that grows on coastal dunes across northern Europe and central Asia. Sharp, oily and high in vitamin C, with a flavour somewhere between passionfruit and pine.
funFact: The berries cling so tightly that traditional harvesting involves freezing whole branches and shaking the fruit off.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or topped with sparkling wine where the acidity does real work. It is tart enough to function as the citrus element in a cocktail rather than only the sweet one.

composition.summary: Sea buckthorn berries macerated in spirit and sweetened.
composition.process: The berries carry oil as well as juice, which gives an unusual weight on the palate.

name: Lingonberry Liqueur
description: Nordic lingonberries steeped in grain spirit — tart, faintly bitter and less sweet than most berry liqueurs. The berry is a Scandinavian staple that grows wild in forest floor across the north.
funFact: Lingonberries keep almost indefinitely without preservation because they are naturally high in benzoic acid.

serve.how: Cold and neat after a meal, or over ice with soda. The tartness makes it useful in cocktails wherever you would otherwise reach for cranberry, with far more depth.

composition.summary: Wild lingonberries macerated in grain spirit and lightly sweetened.
composition.process: Less sugar than most berry liqueurs, which is what keeps the tartness in front.

name: Rum Cream
description: Jamaican rum blended with dairy cream and spice, the Caribbean's answer to Irish cream. Richer and more molasses-driven, and considerably better over ice than its supermarket placement suggests.
funFact: It emerged in the 1970s as Caribbean distillers watched Irish cream take off and reasoned that aged rum would work at least as well as whiskey.

serve.how: Over ice, or in coffee. Shake before pouring. Jamaican rum cream carries more spice than the Irish style, so it works in a Mudslide or over ice cream without needing extra nutmeg.

composition.summary: Aged Jamaican rum emulsified with dairy cream and spice.
composition.process: The rum's ester content is what keeps the fruit note detectable through the dairy.

name: Dulce de Leche Liqueur
description: Argentina's caramelised milk turned into a cream liqueur, thick and sweet enough to be a dessert on its own. A relatively modern product built on the country's most beloved ingredient.
funFact: Argentina and Uruguay have argued for decades over which country invented dulce de leche, and neither has conceded an inch.

serve.how: Cold, neat, in a small glass, or poured over ice cream. It is extremely sweet, so treat it as dessert. It also goes into coffee, which cuts it usefully.

composition.summary: Dulce de leche blended with spirit and cream.
composition.process: Real dulce de leche rather than caramel syrup is what separates the good bottles from the rest.

name: Crema de Orujo
description: Galician pomace spirit blended with cream, coffee and sugar into a pale, sweet liqueur that has quietly become the region's most popular after-dinner drink — outselling the clear orujo it comes from.
funFact: Galician restaurants routinely bring a bottle to the table unasked at the end of a meal, alongside the clear orujo and the herbal one.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer or the fridge, neat, in a small glass. Cold is essential — warm it separates on the palate and the pomace shows through the cream unpleasantly.

composition.summary: Orujo blended with dairy cream, coffee and sugar.
composition.process: The pomace base gives a rougher edge than the Irish cream style, which Galicians consider the point.
